New Hampshire: New Hampshire is a rural colony whose economy depends on farming, fishing, lumber, and shipbuilding. Colonists resent British interference but worry about their ability to sustain a prolonged war and future repercussions from British forces operating out of Canada. New Hampshire wants assurances that the other colonies will provide military assistance to protect its commerce and share the financial burden of independence.
Massachusetts: Massachusetts is among the strongest supporters of independence, having already suffered under British occupation, the closing of Boston Harbor, and the Intolerable Acts. The battles of Lexington and Concord and Bunker Hill have demonstrated the determination of its citizens. Its greatest concern is that the other colonies will abandon Massachusetts and seek a separate reconciliation with the Crown. Massachusetts wants a firm commitment to colonial unity.
Rhode Island: Rhode Island has a prosperous maritime economy that depends heavily on shipping, international commerce, the rum trade and its connection to slavery. Its long tradition of religious liberty and self-government makes British interference unpopular, but the colony's extensive coastline leaves its ports, merchant ships, and communities vulnerable to the powerful British Royal Navy. Rhode Island wants assurances that independence will protect its coastal ports, open new international markets, and preserve its tradition of autonomy.
Connecticut: Connecticut has developed a productive agricultural and commercial economy. Although generally sympathetic to the revolutionary cause, its inhabitants worry about the financial costs, disruption of trade, and the loss of agricultural workers to military service. Connecticut is also concerned that a new American government will interfere with its established political institutions. It wants guarantees that independence will preserve local self-government.
New York: New York is deeply divided between Patriots, Loyalists, and those who still hope for reconciliation with Great Britain. Its merchants depend heavily on British trade and many wealthy landowners fear that a revolution could threaten their property and political influence. New York City and the Hudson River are strategically important and particularly vulnerable to British military occupation. The colony is reluctant to declare independence without adequate military protection and clear authorization from its own political representatives from its provincial government.
New Jersey: New Jersey is situated between the important cities of New York and Philadelphia farms and transportation routes vulnerable to becoming a major battleground. Its population is politically divided, and Royal Governor William Franklin remains loyal to the Crown. Farmers and merchants fear the destruction of property, interruption of commerce, and shortages caused by a prolonged conflict. New Jersey wants assurances that the Continental Army will defend its communities and that the other colonies are fully committed to the revolutionary cause.
Pennsylvania: Pennsylvania is one of the most economically prosperous and diverse colonies. Its merchants benefit from British commerce, while many Quakers oppose warfare on religious grounds. Conservative political leaders fear that independence could produce social unrest and overturn established institutions. Pennsylvania remains divided over whether political reconciliation is still possible. The colony wants evidence that peaceful alternatives have been exhausted and that an independent government can protect religious freedom, commerce, property, and political stability.
Delaware: Delaware is a small colony with limited population, financial resources, and military strength. Its economy depends heavily on agriculture and trade through the Delaware River and nearby Philadelphia. Many inhabitants fear that independence could expose their communities to British naval attacks while leaving them dependent upon their larger neighbors for protection. Delaware's political leaders are divided between immediate independence and continued reconciliation. The colony wants guarantees of military assistance and future economic stability.
Maryland: Maryland's economy depends heavily on tobacco exports and commercial relationships with British merchants. Wealthy landowners and established political families fear that independence could threaten their property, economic interests, and social position. Many colonists are concerned about replacing the existing proprietary government with an uncertain political system and that foreign markets will remain accessible, private property will be protected, and the colony will retain authority over its internal affairs.
Virginia: Virginia is a leading advocate of independence but its economy remains heavily dependent on tobacco exports, British credit, and enslaved labor. Many plantation owners owe substantial debts to British merchants and worry about the economic consequences of severing those relationships. British military activity along the coast and Lord Dunmore's proclamation offering freedom to certain enslaved people who joined British forces have intensified slaveholders' fears. Virginia wants strong colonial unity, access to foreign markets, coastal protection, and assurances that its political and economic institutions will remain under local control.
North Carolina: North Carolina has already demonstrated considerable support for independence through the Halifax Resolves of April 1776. Nevertheless, the colony faces internal divisions between coastal communities, inland settlers, Patriots, and Loyalists. Its largely agricultural economy and limited infrastructure make raising money and supplying an army difficult. Frontier communities also fear conflict with Indigenous nations. North Carolina wants assurances that the other colonies will provide assistance, protect vulnerable settlements, and respect its authority over local affairs.
South Carolina: South Carolina's considerable wealth depends on rice and indigo exports, international commerce, and a plantation economy sustained by slavery. Its political leaders fear that war with Great Britain could destroy valuable trade relationships, expose Charleston to naval attack, and undermine the system upon which their wealth depends. South Carolina wants assurances of coastal defense, access to foreign markets, and continued local control over its economic and social institutions.
Georgia: Georgia is the youngest and one of the least populated of the thirteen colonies. Its limited military resources, and exposed southern and western frontiers make independence risky. Georgia faces potential threats from British-controlled East Florida, as well as conflicts involving Indigenous nations along its frontier. Settlers have benefited from British military protection and fear losing it. Georgia wants firm guarantees that the other colonies will provide military assistance against external threats.
